Efﬁcacy of pregabalin in a case of stiff-person syndrome: Clinical and
neurophysiological evidence
G. Squintani a, T. Bovi b, L. Ferigo a, A.M. Musso a, S. Ottaviani a, G. Moretto a, F. Morgante c,⁎, M. Tinazzi a, b
a UO Neurologia Borgo Trento, Azienda Ospedaliera Universitaria-Integrata, Verona, Italy

Keywords:
Stiff person syndrome
Pregabalin
Neurophysiology
GABA
Cortical silent period
Symptomatic treatment of stiff-person syndrome (SPS) might be challenging and a signi ﬁcant improvement
of stiffness and rigidity is generally reached with high doses of benzodiazepines or baclofen causing side
effects.
A 71-year old woman diagnosed with SPS complained of marked stiffness of trunk and lower limb muscles
with sudden painful spasms. She was unable to walk and she could not lean on her right leg. Cortical silent period
(CSP) duration evaluated from right abductor pollicis brevis (APB) with transcranial magnetic stimulation
was shortened. Polygraphic electromyographic (EMG) evaluation from paraspinal and leg muscles disclosed
continuous motor unit activity at rest with interference muscular pattern. Symptomatic treatment with diazepam
was withdrawn because of excessive sedation. In order to relieve the intense lumbar pain, she was prescribed
pregabalin; since the day after, rigidity and painful spasms dramatically improved and she could walk without
assistance. The clinical bene ﬁt persisted at 3 months follow-up and was paralleled by almost complete
disappearance of EMG activity at rest and prolongation of CSP. The clinical and electrophysiological
data in this SPS patient suggest the possible ef ﬁcacy of pregabalin as symptomatic treatment without
any signi ﬁcant side effects, which needs to be replicated in larger case series.

1. Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurological autoimmune
disorder characterized by stiffness and rigidity in axial and proximal
limb muscles, conditioning lumbar hyperlordosis and dif ﬁculty in
bending or turning [1]. SPS recognizes an autoimmune pathogenesis
targeting GABA transmission as supported by the presence of highly
speciﬁc antibodies against the 65-kDa isoform of glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD-65), the rate-limiting enzyme for the synthesis
of GABA [2].
Therapeutic strategies of SPS are usually directed to different
goals: immunotherapy and/or symptomatic treatment by stimulating
γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) transmission [1]. Although diazepam is
widely used as symptomatic treatment, a signi ﬁcant improvement
of stiffness and rigidity is generally reached with high doses and
side effects, including sedation and somnolence.
2. Case report
We report a patient with SPS and anti-GAD antibodies who
showed a sustained beneﬁcial response to pregabalin. Written informed
consent for the video was obtained.
A 71-year-old woman was admitted to our neurology division
complaining of marked stiffness of trunk and lower limb muscles
with sudden painful spasms, started eight months before. She suffered

APB = 6.3 ms; left APB = 5.4 ms) and the lower limbs (right
AH = 16.1 ms; left AH = 15.2 ms). Cortical silent period (CSP) duration,
obtained with TMS, was recorded from the right APB at ~ 15% of
maximum voluntary contraction by stimulating at an intensity of
130% of the resting motor threshold. CSP duration was 20 ms, as
measured from the MEP onset to the initial return of EMG activity
(Fig. 1 A). Serum anti-GAD-65 antibodies were signi ﬁcantly increased
(47 nmol/l, reference values b1). Paraneoplastic anti-amphiphisine
antibodies were absent. Thyroid stimulating hormone and anti-
thyreoperoxidasis antibodies titer were elevated. Routine cerebrospinal
ﬂuid analysis was normal and included testing of total protein, albumin,
immunoglobulins, glucose, lactate, cell count, cytological staining, and
investigation of infectious diseases. Brain magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) was normal; spinal cord MRI showed lumbar disk protrusions
without spinal cord compression. Diagnosis of autoimmune SPS was
made based on clinical, electrophysiological and immunological
ﬁndings. Diazepam was effective for muscle stiffness but it was
withdrawn for excessive sedation. In order to relieve the intense
lumbar pain, she was prescribed pregabalin (75 mg, twice a day). The
day after, rigidity and painful spasms dramatically improved and she
could walk without assistance (Appendix A, video, segment B); the
clinical beneﬁt was paralleled by a signi ﬁcant decrease of continuous
motor unit activity at the EMG. A trial with tramadol and indomethacin
reduced pain but neither improved gait, involuntary spasms and stiffness,
nor modulated continuous motor unit activity. Before discharge, we
increased pregabalin up to 300 mg/day. At 3 months follow-up, she
still reported the improvement on rigidity and spasms; gait and
osteotendinous re ﬂexes were normal and there were bilateral ﬂexor
plantar responses. EMG activity at rest almost disappeared and CSP
duration increased up to 60 ms ( Fig. 1 B). She did not complain of
any side effect, speci ﬁcally dizziness or sedation.
3. Discussion
This patient with SPS showed a clear improvement of gait and a
reduction of muscle stiffness and involuntary spasms after treatment
with pregabalin. Clinical bene ﬁt was paralleled by an improvement of
electrophysiological data.
Autoimmune-mediated impairment of GABAergic inhibition, at
spinal and cortical level, has been proposed as a major pathogenetic
mechanism of muscles stiffness in SPS [4]. TMS studies in SPS demon-
strated decreased intracortical inhibition and shortened CSP [5,6],
consistent with GABA
A and GABA B impaired transmission [6,7], and
increased intracortical facilitation, compatible with enhancement of
glutammatergic transmission [8]. Besides to drugs enhancing GABA
neurotransmission, SPS symptoms can be treated by anti-epileptics[1]
such as gabapentin [9]. Pregabalin is an antiepileptic with a chemical
structure similar to GABA [10] but it is not a GABA-mimetic nor does
it bind to GABA A or GABAB receptors. It is thought to inhibit calcium
inﬂux and subsequent release of excitatory neurotransmitters, including
glutamate and norepinephrine[10]. As a possible mechanism of action
in SPS, pregabalin might have compensated the imbalance between
inhibitory and excitatory intracortical circuits. This hypothesis is sup-
ported by the prolongation of the GABAB mediated CSP after pregabalin

introduction. Interestingly, similarly to osteotendinous reﬂexes, plantar
responses were normalized after 3 months treatment. Extensor plantar
response were occasionally reported in SPS [11,12], possibly reﬂecting
the enhancement of exteroceptive reﬂexes which is a neurophysiological
hallmark of SPS [1]. One possible explanation of inverted plantar
responses is that pregabalin might have reduced pathological
enhancement of exteroceptive re ﬂexes by supraspinal modulation
of GABA-ergic transmission.
We acknowledge it is not possible to de ﬁnitely establish a direct
role of pregabalin on SPS symptoms in this single case report. Indeed,

beneﬁt of pregabalin might be also related to its analgesic properties
[10] as pain is a constant feature of SPS; yet, this is unlikely since
tramadol and indomethacin just reduced pain, but did not decrease
continuous motor unit activity which sustained muscle stiffness.
Moreover, it should be recognized that SPS symptoms can beﬂuctuating
and a placebo effect might have occurred. Finally, anti-anxiety
properties of pregabalin [13] might have concurred to its bene ﬁt
given the frequent comorbidity of anxiety and phobias in SPS [14].
In conclusion, the clinical and electrophysiological improvement
after pregabalin in this SPS patients support further investigation to
explore its effectiveness in a large series of patients.
